Rule: Three pillars with three data contracts: LokMat (8 AM, culture, fun, growth engine), JanMat (8 PM, local civic delivery, mapped by seat), RashtraMat (Sunday 8 PM, national policy opinion, state/national display only, never a seat map). RashtraMat is a proposed name; if you prefer two pillars, label it 'JanMat: National Opinion'.
Why / what it fixes: v1 mixed foreign policy, ideology, lifestyle and civic delivery under one JanMat label, which undercuts the 'no political shouting matches' promise.

Rule: JanMat is a tracker, not a quiz. 14 core questions repeat every 4 weeks with identical wording; 10 rotating module slots per cycle carry quarterly, bi-annual and annual modules. A cycle is 28 days: 24 JanMat evenings (Mon-Sat) plus 4 Sundays for RashtraMat.
Why / what it fixes: Identical re-asks are what turn answers into a seat-level time series. v1 repeated only a handful of items and several had no dates.

Rule: Count quorum per question over a window, not per day: 28 days for trackers, 84 days for modules, 7 days for LokMat. Publish in tiers: 250 'Early signal', 1,000 'Reliable', 2,500 'Robust'. Always show n.
Why / what it fixes: One question per day x 543 seats x 250 votes is about 1.4 lakh verified answers a day just to light a single day's map. A rolling window makes quorum reachable.

Rule: JanMat asks only about verifiable local service experience: roads, power, water, waste, safety, policing, health, schools, transport, government services, livelihood, prices. Lifestyle, personal finance and ideology move to LokMat or RashtraMat.
Why / what it fixes: Constituency maps only mean something where the service is local. 159 v1 JanMat rows included cinema, Reels time, marriage format, equity outlook and hard-water hair.

Rule: One idea per question, about 20 words or fewer, an explicit reference period ('this month', 'last visit'), balanced anchors, 3 options by default (2-4 max), option labels of 5 words or fewer, and a 'Haven't used / Not applicable' option for service questions, excluded from the base.
Why / what it fixes: v1 had double-barrelled items ('responsiveness and conduct', 'performance and accessibility'), loaded options, and options up to 90 characters, too long for a one-tap, one-minute mobile flow.

Rule: Contested political topics: neutral wording, a 'Not sure' option, State/National display only, High sensitivity flag, ethics-panel review, and election-silence suppression. Ask about offices ('State Government', 'your MP's work'), never name a living politician in a question or option.
Why / what it fixes: The website hero ballot asks 'Would you re-elect Narendra Modi in 2029?'. That is vote-intention polling on a named leader, and it contradicts 'non-partisan' and 'perception index'.

Rule: Foreign policy and history go to RashtraMat or Itihas Ki Adalat only, at most one per month, with a historians' panel and a preference for pre-1990 events. Events like Kandahar, 1971, 1962, demonetisation, the Indus treaty and the Navy/Pakistan items are parked.
Why / what it fixes: These ride on strong emotions and invite brigading from outside the seat, which defeats seat-level maps.

Rule: Priority re-scored 1-5 (5 = launch hook or core tracker). Low-fit, duplicate or metro-skewed items are parked, not deleted; see the change log for every v1 row.
Why / what it fixes: 65 of 288 v1 Casual rows were rated 1-2, and many near-duplicates (Messi/Ronaldo/Real/Barca/F1/NBA/MMA/boxing) fought for the same slot.

Rule: No private-brand comparison questions at launch (telecom, quick commerce, payment apps, banks, retailers). Revisit later as a labelled consumer-trust series with disclosure rules.
Why / what it fixes: 'No ads, no data sales' is a core promise. Brand duels attract sponsorship pressure and legal risk.

Rule: Correct the metro skew: every cricket question is balanced by non-cricket content; added festivals, regional food, kabaddi/hockey/kushti, farm and village life, regional music. Target at least 40% of LokMat questions that a village resident and a metro resident can answer equally well.
Why / what it fixes: The deck promises 'free from elite metropolitan bias'. v1 had 1 festival item, 1 traditional-sports item and almost no rural life, but several Premier League, anime, Marvel and Nolan questions.

Rule: Hinglish is the default display. Before launch add Hindi (Devanagari) and the major regional languages, translated by native reviewers and back-translated for meaning parity.
Why / what it fixes: v1 had one row with Devanagari. Darbhanga, Belagavi and Nagpur voters will not all answer in Roman Hindi.

Rule: JanMat and RashtraMat require OTP. LokMat votes count on the seat map only from OTP-verified accounts. Email-only LokMat votes may count toward personal badges, not public maps.
Why / what it fixes: The website lets LokMat run on email/social sign-up while the same seat map and Gold Points exist, so bots can farm points through LokMat.

Rule: Gold Points (needed to change seats) are earned only from OTP-verified activity, rate-capped, with manual review for swing seats. Keep the 15 Aug and 26 Jan free resets. Do not mix this with referral-based seat changes (the deck and site disagree).
Why / what it fixes: A bot farming points on LokMat could relocate into a swing seat and then vote on JanMat.

Rule: Replace 'hash and discard the phone number' with a keyed HMAC for the participation token (secret in an HSM). Blur and batch timestamps between Room A and Room B, log no IP or device data against ballots, set a minimum cohort before display, open-source the ballot logic, and get an independent audit.
Why / what it fixes: A plain hash of a 10-digit mobile number can be brute-forced. 'Technically impossible' and '100%' language invites a single counterexample to damage the brand.

Rule: The receipt proves participation, never choice, so it cannot be used for coercion or vote-selling. Put the LokMat/JanMat history difference in one comparison table so the two promises never collide.
Why / what it fixes: The deck shows a Vote ID receipt; the About page says 'no one, not even the user, can see past selections'.

Rule: Optional age/gender/rural-urban declaration; post-stratify to Census, NFHS and electoral-roll benchmarks; publish who answered; show organic vs referred share; flag referral-chain clusters.
Why / what it fixes: Verified is not representative. 250 self-selected responses is a signal, not a poll of 18 lakh electors.

Rule: Every JanMat question carries a suggested external benchmark; run a pilot comparison and publish calibration, including where BhuMat is wrong.
Why / what it fixes: Gives sceptics a reason to cite BhuMat. Confirm each dataset exists and is current before relying on it.

Rule: Observe election-silence windows (RP Act s.126(1)(b): no display of opinion-poll results in the 48 hours before polling closes; s.126A covers exit polls). No vote-intention questions. Replace the hero ballot on the homepage.
Why / what it fixes: Constituency-level political sentiment near an election is regulated; get legal review before each cycle.

Rule: Public nominations feed a moderation queue (the Suggest a Poll form); an independent advisory panel reviews Medium/High items; wording for High items is published 7 days ahead; options are balanced and neutral.
Why / what it fixes: Agenda-setting is the real power in any poll. The deck answers 'who decides what 1.4 billion think?' without saying who decides the questions.

Rule: Dates are anchored to launch day (Tue 26 Jan 2027). If launch moves, shift every date by the same number of days. A reserve evening each month is left for rapid-response civic questions (floods, outages, exam leaks).
Why / what it fixes: v1 dates started 2 Oct 2026, nearly 4 months before the stated launch, and only 37 rows had dates.

Rule: First impressions should come from Low-sensitivity JanMat items (roads, power, women's safety) rather than geopolitics. Day 1-7 roadmap on the site should be rebuilt from this bank.
Why / what it fixes: The site's Day 1-7 roadmap leads with the Navy in the Gulf of Aden, a Leader of the Opposition rating, and aid to Pakistan.

Rule: Label any prototype map as simulated data. Do not describe the pre-registration count as verified votes. Publish a methodology page, a privacy policy and terms before collecting more personal data (footer links currently point to #privacy and #terms).
Why / what it fixes: DPDP core duties are phased in over about 18 months from late 2025 (around May 2027); a published notice and consent flow should exist from the first sign-up.

Rule: Year-end awards run 1-28 Dec 2027, one per morning, with 3-4 named nominees chosen from public nominations in November, and results on 31 Dec. 'Union Ministry' and 'State' awards are Medium sensitivity.
Why / what it fixes: v1 BOTY options were abstract archetypes ('Large-Scale Action Production'), which cannot be voted on.

Rule: The bank is sized for about 154 daily LokMat days (to 28 Jun 2027), 24-evening JanMat cycles, and 18 RashtraMat Sundays. Refresh LokMat quarterly; hold back about 20% of slots for trending topics.
Why / what it fixes: One-time questions run out; the tracker spine keeps the product valuable after the novelty fades.
